source.authors: Rojas V, Labra A, Valdés JL, Velásquez NA
source.title: Females of the four-eyed frog, Pleurodema thaul (Anura, Leptodactylidae), respond behaviourally to conspecific male scent

value: wild-caught females spent significantly longer in the Y-maze arm with conspecific male-scent water than in the distilled-water control arm (sign test Z = 2.33, p < 0.05); first arm entered did not differ from chance (one-tailed binomial p = 0.385)
units: categorical (time in scent arm versus control arm over 60 trials; first-arm choice)
method: Y-maze double-choice: along the floor of one arm (15 x 10 x 10 cm) a scent trail of 5 ml of water from the aquarium of a male that had been acoustically stimulated (advertisement call broadcast for one hour in darkness on 10 consecutive nights; water stored at 4 C for three days), in the other arm 5 ml of distilled water; gate lifted and the female's reaction monitored for five minutes; first choice (first arm entered) and permanence time in each arm scored
conditions: wild-sourced: 13 adults (3 males as scent donors, 10 females as test subjects) collected at Puente Negro, central Chile (34 40 S, 70 53 W), returned to their collecting point afterwards, SAG permit 5641 and university ethics approval printed; collection date not printed; 10 females each tested 6 times (twice with the scent of each of the 3 males) = 60 trials, so trials are repeated measures on 10 females; position of the two solutions interchanged to avoid position bias, no other randomisation described; same-section nulls: although females entered the male-scent arm first in about 80 per cent of trials, first-arm choice did not differ from chance (binomial p = 0.385); permanence-time responses were consistent between replicates (Mann-Whitney Z = -0.483, p = 0.629) and did not differ among the three male donors (Kruskal-Wallis H = 2.736, p = 0.741); no means or medians of permanence time printed; scent was male-aquarium water after call stimulation, so the paper does not separate male chemical cues from any effect of the calling treatment; single control (distilled water), no heterospecific or other-sex scent comparator
quote: Our data suggest that females are capable of responding behaviourally to male scents, since they spent longer periods in the zones with male scent, rather than in zones with water.
note: Classification: behavioural_response, choice and permanence of wild-caught females at male-scent versus water control in a Y-maze; the permanence-time effect is significant and the first-choice effect is null, so the value is protocol-specific and keeps both. source.authors: Haswell PM, Jones KA, Kusak J, Hayward MW
source.title: Fear, foraging and olfaction: how mesopredators avoid costly interactions with apex predators

value: foxes left significantly more food (higher giving-up density) at patches with wolf-urine granules than at mint-scented control patches (14.98 vs 11.16 food pieces left; F1,93 = 17.243, P < 0.001); foxes also spent more time in major vigilance (30.30 vs 18.83 per cent, P < 0.001) and less time foraging (44.09 vs 55.48 per cent, P = 0.017)
units: food pieces left in a patch at departure (giving-up density, mean ± SD); percent of visit time
method: field giving-up-density experiment with automated cameras: each site had six patches (2 x 3 grid, 60 m apart), each a 14 L bucket half-sunk in the ground holding 20 pieces (80 g) of dog food mixed into 8 L of sieved substrate; day 1 untreated, from day 2 a control of 25 g sand scented with 3 ml peppermint extract on a 15 x 15 cm moss piece 15 cm from the bucket, from day 7 the control was removed and 25 g of commercial wolf-urine granules placed in the same spot for five days
conditions: wild-sourced: free-ranging red foxes in mixed beech and fir forest, Plitvice Lakes National Park, Croatia, July to September 2015; 12 sites attempted, foxes foraged at 3, which were repeated in late August; 195 GUD measures (127 wolf urine, 68 control); individual foxes could not be identified, so the number of foxes is unknown and repeated visits by the same animals are treated with a random effect for patch location; treatment order was fixed (control days before urine days within each cycle), not randomised, so treatment is confounded with time within the cycle; wolf-urine source (captive or wild wolves) not stated, commercial product PredatorPee; same-section secondary results: total daily visit duration shorter under wolf urine (132.59 vs 269.14 s, P = 0.01) and time sniffing the ground higher (12.48 vs 6.85 per cent, P = 0.025); nulls: soil penetration, percent visibility to road and moon illumination had no effect on GUD (P = 0.54, 0.17, 0.39), visit frequency and minor vigilance were unaffected by any variable; control is a minty odour, not a no-odour or non-predator urine control
quote: GUDs were significantly higher (less food harvested from patches) during wolf urine treatment (14.98 ± 6.94 SD, N = 127) than under the control treatment (mint, 11.16 ± 7.10 SD, N = 68).
note: Classification: behavioural_response, foraging-cost response of wild foxes to apex-predator urine against a mint-odour control; scent is the only manipulated stimulus but foxes' vigilance and GUD may be driven by other cues in the urine product.
